title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E740 looks for a space (non-planar) curve, described by its two projections y(x) and z(x), that makes ∫V dx a maximum or minimum. V may depend on x, y, z and on derivatives of y and z of any order. Euler sets p = y', q = y'', r = y''' and p' = z', q' = z'', r' = z''', and sets aside any integral formulas that might occur inside V.

On this page he writes the total differential
dV = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + … + N' dz + P' dp' + Q' dq' + R' dr' + …
In modern terms, N = V_y, P = V_{y'}, Q = V_{y''}, and N' = V_z, P' = V_{z'}, and so on.

§6 recalls the result for one unknown function from his Methodus inveniendi (1744). With z absent, the extremal satisfies the higher-order Euler–Lagrange (Euler–Poisson) equation
N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − d³R/dx³ + … = 0.
By symmetry, with y absent the condition is
N' − dP'/dx + d²Q'/dx² − … = 0.

§7 begins the reduction of the two-function problem to the one-function case. Treat the projection z(x) as already known. All z-terms in dV can then be absorbed into the M dx term, so the ordinary one-variable method gives the y-equation. The next page does the same with y fixed and concludes that both Euler–Lagrange equations must hold simultaneously.

In modern language: the first variation of a functional of a vector function (y, z) vanishes iff each component's partial variation vanishes. This gives the system of Euler–Lagrange equations, one per unknown function.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The coordinate-wise argument (vary y with z fixed, then z with y fixed) gives exactly the correct necessary conditions, because the variations δy and δz are independent.

Typographical: the second line of dV should be read as continuing the first with a '+' sign (… + N'∂z + P'∂p' + …). In the scan the prime on N in that line and in the second Euler equation is faint or possibly missing.
The second displayed equation omits the trailing 'etc.' present in the first, a minor inconsistency.
On the next page the printed equations contain typos: ∂x² for ∂x³, and Q, R for Q', R' in §8.

ideas.what: Notation for the total differential of the integrand with respect to all derivatives of two unknown functions
ideas.modern_name: Partial derivatives V_y, V_{y'}, …, V_z, V_{z'}, … of a Lagrangian depending on higher derivatives
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi, 1744) for the one-function version

ideas.what: Higher-order Euler–Lagrange equation N − P' + Q'' − R''' … = 0
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler 1744 (Poisson's name for the higher-order form)

ideas.what: Extremals of functionals of two unknown functions (space curves) obey one Euler equation per function, obtained by varying each projection separately
ideas.modern_name: System of Euler–Lagrange equations for vector-valued functions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760s, δ-method), and Euler himself in earlier treatments
ideas.where_published: Also implicit in Euler's 1771 variational-calculus papers (E385 etc.) and Lagrange's Miscellanea Taurinensia 1760–61; this paper is E740

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, correct derivation of the Euler–Lagrange system for two dependent variables by coordinate-wise reduction. It was well known by then (Lagrange 1760) and is documented in histories of the calculus of variations.
transcription_corrections: Second line of the dV formula: read '+ N'∂z + P'∂p' + Q'∂q' + R'∂r' etc.' as the continuation of the first line. The prime on N is faint in the scan, which reads 'N.∂z'.
Second Euler equation: the scan appears to show 'N' with a faint or missing prime; it should be N'.
'dein-ceps' is hyphenated across lines in the image (dein- / ceps), and 'memo-ratas' likewise; the transcription merges these correctly.
